DOCUMENT:
Evaluation Report: Text-Message Reminders in the School Flu Vaccination Programme, 2025-26
Eastvale Public Health Team, February 2026

1. Summary
This report evaluates the use of text-message reminders to parents during the 2025-26 school-aged flu vaccination programme in Eastvale. Uptake was 13 percentage points higher in schools using reminders than in schools that did not. We recommend that reminders be extended to every primary school in the area for 2026-27, with the aim of raising uptake to at least 70% across Eastvale.

2. Background
Children in Reception to Year 6 are offered a nasal flu vaccine in school each autumn. Parents must return a consent form, on paper or through the online consent portal, before the immunisation team visits. Low consent return is the main reason children go unvaccinated: in most schools nearly all children with consent are vaccinated on the day.

In 2025-26, schools could opt in to an automated reminder service. Parents who had not returned consent received up to three text messages in the two weeks before the session, each with a link to the online portal. 38 of Eastvale's 92 primary schools opted in. Opting-in schools were disproportionately those with a full-time school nurse (29 of the 38, compared with 11 of the other 54) and those in the more affluent western half of the area.

3. Results
Table 1. Uptake by reminder status, 2025-26
Group | Schools | Eligible pupils | Consents returned | Vaccinated | Uptake
Reminder schools | 38 | 9,120 | 6,840 | 6,384 | 70.0%
Non-reminder schools | 54 | 12,960 | 7,970 | 7,388 | 57.0%
All schools | 92 | 22,080 | 14,810 | 13,772 | 66.0%

Consent return was 75% in reminder schools and 61% in non-reminder schools. In both groups more than 92% of children with consent were vaccinated, confirming that consent, not attendance on the day, is the binding constraint.

Overall uptake across Eastvale was 66.0%, above the national ambition of 65% for this age group for the first time.

The 13-point difference between reminder and non-reminder schools is the clearest evidence we have on what drives uptake locally. It shows that text reminders raise uptake by around 13 percentage points, more than any other intervention we have tried, at a cost of less than ten pence per message.

4. Who is not being reached
Uptake in non-reminder schools varied widely, from 38% to 79%. The lowest-uptake schools are concentrated in the eastern wards, which have higher proportions of families who speak a language other than English at home and higher rates of household mobility. In the 54 non-reminder schools, the school information system holds a valid mobile number for 61% of families, compared with 93% in the reminder schools. Paper consent forms in these schools are also more often returned incomplete, typically with the medical history section blank.

Immunisation team staff report that a second visit (a "mop-up" session) adds between three and six points of uptake where it is offered, but mop-up sessions were held in only 14 schools this year because of staffing.

5. Cost
Each reminder costs £0.08 to send. If all three reminders were sent to every family without consent in the 54 non-reminder schools (about 4,990 families on 2025-26 figures), the cost would be under £1,200 a year. Continuing reminders in the existing 38 schools costs about £550 a year. There is a one-off set-up charge of £2,500 for linking school data to the messaging platform.

6. Recommendation
Because reminders raised uptake by 13 points, extending them to the 54 non-reminder schools should raise uptake there from 57% to around 70%, bringing every part of Eastvale up to the level now seen in the west. This is by far the cheapest route to closing the gap. We recommend that the Health and Wellbeing Board fund reminders for all 92 schools from September 2026, at a total first-year cost of under £5,000, and that the team report on uptake by school at the end of the 2026-27 season.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [arithmetic] at: "Overall uptake across Eastvale was 66.0%, above the national ambition of 65% for this age group for the first time." -- 13,772 vaccinated / 22,080 eligible = 62.4%, not 66.0% (the table's 'All schools' uptake is also wrong). Correctly computed, Eastvale is below, not above, the 65% ambition.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "It shows that text reminders raise uptake by around 13 percentage points, more than any other intervention we have tried" -- Schools self-selected into reminders, and the document states opting-in schools were disproportionately those with a full-time school nurse (29/38 vs 11/54) and more affluent. The 13-point gap is confounded and cannot be attributed to the reminders.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "extending them to the 54 non-reminder schools should raise uptake there from 57% to around 70%" -- The projection assumes reminders will reach families in the non-reminder schools as they did elsewhere, but the document reports a valid mobile number for only 61% of those families (vs 93% in reminder schools). The recommendation never addresses that roughly 39% of families could not receive a text.

REVIEW:
# Review: Text-Message Reminders in the School Flu Vaccination Programme, 2025-26

The report answers a useful question with good data: the immunisation team's own records, a full season, and all 92 schools. Most of the arithmetic in Table 1 is correct, and the cost figures hold up. But it has one factual error that reverses a headline claim. Its central causal claim is also not supported by the design, and section 4 contains evidence that undercuts the recommendation. Your summary says you looked hard for reasons not to scale and found none. The reasons are in the report itself.

## 1. The overall uptake figure is wrong: Eastvale did not reach 65%

The "All schools" row gives 13,772 vaccinated out of 22,080 eligible. That is **62.4%**, not 66.0%. The two group rows check out:

| Group | Calculation | Uptake |
|---|---|---|
| Reminder schools | 6,384 ÷ 9,120 | 70.0% ✓ |
| Non-reminder schools | 7,388 ÷ 12,960 | 57.0% ✓ |
| All schools | 13,772 ÷ 22,080 | **62.4%** (reported as 66.0%) |

The total row cannot be 66% under any weighting. Even the simple average of the two groups is only 63.5%. So the statement that Eastvale exceeded the 65% national ambition "for the first time" is false. Eastvale is about 2.6 points short. This needs correcting in section 3 and in any briefing. It also changes the framing: this is not building on success, and the gap to the 70% target is about 8 points, not 4.

## 2. The 13-point gap does not show what reminders achieve

The report says the comparison "shows that text reminders raise uptake by around 13 percentage points". It shows no such thing. The two groups differ in many ways besides reminders.

- **Schools chose whether to take part.** Schools that opt in to an optional initiative tend to be more organised and more engaged with immunisation anyway.
- **School nurses are a major confounder.** 76% of reminder schools (29 of 38) have a full-time school nurse, compared with 20% of non-reminder schools (11 of 54). A nurse chasing consent forms in person would plausibly raise consent return without any texts.
- **The groups differ in affluence and geography.** Reminder schools are mostly in the more affluent west. Non-reminder schools are mostly in the east, which has more families who speak another language at home and more household mobility. All of these factors are independently linked to vaccine uptake.
- **There is no baseline.** The report does not say what these same schools achieved in 2024-25, before reminders. If the reminder schools were already about 10 points ahead, the true effect could be small or zero.
- **Mop-up sessions are not accounted for.** These add 3–6 points where they happen, and only 14 schools had one. The report does not say which group those 14 schools were in. If most were reminder schools, that alone could explain part of the gap.

The 13 points is an upper bound mixed together with several other differences. It is not an effect size. The claim that reminders work "more than any other intervention we have tried" also has no supporting comparison in the report.

## 3. Section 4 says the projection for non-reminder schools is unrealistic

The recommendation assumes the 54 schools will move from 57% to about 70%. The report's own findings argue against that.

- **Fewer families can be texted.** Only 61% of families in non-reminder schools have a valid mobile number on record, compared with 93% in reminder schools. About two in five families could not receive a reminder at all. Even if reminders worked as well there, the effect would be diluted by roughly a third. And it probably would not work as well, for the reasons below.
- **Language.** The messages are presumably in English, and many families in the eastern wards speak another language at home.
- **The barrier is not only forgetting.** Paper forms in these schools often come back incomplete, with the medical history section blank. A reminder that links to a portal does not solve problems with literacy, language or understanding the form.
- **Household mobility.** Contact details go out of date faster in these areas.
- **Variation between schools.** Uptake in non-reminder schools ranges from 38% to 79%, so some already exceed 70% without reminders. The low-uptake schools are exactly those where the barriers above are concentrated.

The claim that this brings "every part of Eastvale up to the level now seen in the west" therefore does not follow. The schools furthest behind are the ones where reminders are least likely to reach families or to help.

## 4. The cost analysis is sound but answers the wrong question

The arithmetic is correct:

| Item | Calculation | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| New schools | 4,990 × 3 × £0.08 | ≈ £1,198 |
| Existing schools | 2,280 × 3 × £0.08 | ≈ £547 |
| One-off set-up | | £2,500 |
| **Total** | | **≈ £4,245** (under £5,000) |

Two qualifications apply.

- **It is not cautious for the existing schools.** The 2,280 is the number of families still without consent *after* reminders. The pool of families who were actually texted was larger, so this line is understated. It is cautious for the new schools only because 39% of those families cannot be texted. That is not a saving; it is the reach problem in section 3.
- **The relevant figure is cost per extra child vaccinated.** The low total is real, but it does not show that this is "by far the cheapest route" to closing the gap. That would require comparing it with other options, such as mop-up sessions, translated or simplified consent forms, cleaning up contact data, or school-nurse follow-up. The data on nurses and mop-ups in this report suggests those options may matter more in the eastern schools.

## 5. Smaller points

- The background says reminders went out "in the two weeks before the session". It would help to report delivery data: messages sent and delivered, and portal clicks. This would show whether consents in reminder schools actually came through the reminder link.
- The 92% vaccinated-given-consent figure supports consent being the bottleneck. That is a sound finding. But it does not show that *reminders* are the lever for raising consent.

## Suggested changes

1. Correct overall uptake to 62.4% and remove the claim about the national ambition.
2. Describe the 13-point gap as an association, and list the confounders explicitly.
3. Add 2024-25 uptake for both groups. Compare *change* over time (a difference-in-differences analysis). Adjust or stratify by school nurse, deprivation, ward, and mop-up status.
4. Revise the 70% projection to reflect 61% mobile coverage, or drop it.
5. Reframe the recommendation. Reminders are cheap and worth extending. But for 2026-27, roll them out in a staggered way, or randomise the order in which schools start, so the effect can actually be measured.
6. Alongside the reminders, address the eastern barriers directly:
   - updating contact data,
   - translated messages and forms,
   - support for completing the medical history section,
   - more mop-up sessions.
7. Report cost per additional child vaccinated, not just total cost.

The core message for the Board should be: reminders are inexpensive and probably help, but this evaluation cannot tell us by how much. On their own, they are unlikely to close the east–west gap.
